evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document would primarily serve clinical researchers and trial sponsors designing persistent Lyme disease (PLD) studies, by letting them see how specific eligibility criteria (CDC surveillance definition, Rash/Western-blot requirement, exclusion of prior CFS/FMS or psychiatric misdiagnosis, exclusion of coinfections, functional-impairment thresholds) each reduce recruitable sample size and how combinations compound that reduction. Patient advocates could use the same figures to explain, in plain terms, why trials often fail to represent ~90% of people like them. It would have limited direct relevance to payers/policy audiences since the document contains no cost, insurance-claims, or expenditure data - only recruitment-yield and clinical/functional burden figures.
use_cases: Trial designers and sponsors could use a simulator built from this document's stepwise eligibility-criteria data to estimate how adding or removing specific exclusion criteria (CFS/FMS misdiagnosis exclusion, coinfection exclusion, CDC surveillance definition requirement) changes projected PLD trial sample yield and recruitment timeline, before finalizing a trial protocol.

Because this document is itself about clinical trial/cohort eligibility design, a simulator built from it could prompt researchers to screen enrolled PLD/ALD participants for home environmental exposures (mold, mildew, pet dander) before attributing observed treatment-response variance to the studied drug, since unscreened exposure differences between cohort members could otherwise confound drug-response comparisons.

Patient advocacy groups could use the misdiagnosis and disability figures (e.g., 40% PLD CFS/FMS misdiagnosis, 28% PLD work disability) to illustrate, to clinicians or policymakers, the gap between the clinical PLD population and the narrow population actually studied in RCTs.

package.documentation:
This simulator is based on Johnson et al. (Healthcare, 2025), a peer-reviewed analysis of the MyLymeData patient registry (Phase 2, August 2022) comparing patients who self-identified as having persistent Lyme disease (PLD, n=3,589) versus acute Lyme disease (ALD, n=594). The document reports no dollar-denominated cost data; all figures here describe diagnostic, functional, and clinical-trial-recruitment burden only.

The three trial-yield inputs come from the document's Section 3.3 description of a smaller 'Attrition Sample' (PLD n=2,396; ALD n=400) that excludes missing/'don't know' survey responses. The document reports cumulative yields of 64%, then 39%, then 10% as three criteria are applied in sequence (clinical diagnosis + symptom severity + lab test; then excluding prior chronic fatigue syndrome/fibromyalgia misdiagnosis; then excluding diagnosed coinfections). The two retention-fraction inputs were derived by dividing those cumulative figures (39/64 and 10/39); the document does not state these per-step fractions directly, so this is a decomposition of the document's own sequential filtering, not a value it reports itself. The cited 'other-disease' benchmark (65%) comes from a different disease area (pulmonary arterial hypertension trials, Hill et al. 2008) and is not Lyme-specific.

Both differences were statistically significant in the source. PLD and ALD groups are self-identified, cross-sectional labels from the same survey administration, not matched longitudinal cohorts; the document states a direct symptom comparison at one follow-up point is not possible with this data.

The Table 2 burden figures used here are pooled by disease-stage subgroup only; they have not been checked for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity in this document, though the document separately reports the PLD subgroup was more likely to be female than the ALD subgroup (81% vs 76%, p=0.0053). Federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports disaggregated analysis of this kind even though this document did not perform it. The document also describes a systemic gap between PLD research and clinical practice: commonly used trial eligibility criteria, including the CDC surveillance case definition (described by a CDC official as 'too restrictive for clinical diagnosis'), exclude roughly 90% of the clinically diagnosed PLD population studied here, which the authors link to a lack of clinical treatment guidance.

scenarios.description: Lowering the coinfection retention fraction to an illustrative lower bound (0.1) shows the compounded PLD trial yield falling further below the document's reported 10%.

scenarios.label: Higher other-disease benchmark yield
scenarios.goal: Tests how much larger the yield gap would appear using an illustrative higher other-disease benchmark.
scenarios.description: Raising the comparator yield to an illustrative higher value (80%) makes the PLD-yield-minus-benchmark gap more negative, showing PLD yield further below an assumed higher benchmark.
